vignette:
The Weight of Air

Miriam is sixty years old and has spent the better part of her adult life in the company of beginnings — the first cry of a newborn, the exhausted relief on a new mother's face, the particular hush that falls over a delivery room in those first trembling seconds of life. She has been a midwife for thirty-two years, and she has always believed that her work is fundamentally about trust: a woman trusts her body, trusts the process, trusts Miriam. That sense of trust was shattered three years ago in a hospital storage corridor that smelled, at first, of nothing at all.

It happened during what should have been an unremarkable Tuesday afternoon shift. A maintenance error in an adjacent supply room caused the release of a concentrated industrial cleaning agent — a chlorine-based compound — into the ventilation system serving the corridor where Miriam was retrieving equipment. She noticed a faint chemical sharpness in the air seconds before her throat began to close. By the time the alarm sounded, she was on her knees, eyes streaming, unable to draw a full breath. She was found by a colleague, her lips tinged blue, and was taken to the emergency department by stretcher. She spent four days in hospital, two of them on supplemental oxygen, and was told she was fortunate.

Miriam does not feel fortunate.

In the months that followed, her lungs healed well enough, according to the pulmonologist's charts. But something else did not heal. She began waking at three in the morning, heart hammering, certain she cannot breathe — certain, in those first disoriented seconds, that she is back on the floor of that corridor. She lies still, counting her own inhales, trying to persuade her body that the air is safe. Her partner, a quiet and steady man named Pieter, has learned to simply hold her hand without speaking until the shaking passes. She is grateful for this, and also ashamed that it is necessary.

Cleaning products are now a serious problem. The scent of bleach — in a supermarket aisle, in a public bathroom, on the ward where she still works — triggers an immediate and total response: her chest tightens, her vision narrows, and she is flooded with a certainty of dying that she knows, intellectually, is disproportionate, but cannot talk herself out of. She has begun taking longer routes through the hospital to avoid the housekeeping trolleys. She carries the knowledge of their schedules in her head like a second timetable.

At work, she functions — mostly. Her colleagues would describe her as experienced, capable, a little quieter than she used to be. What they do not see is the effort it costs her to enter the building each morning, or the way she scans every room she enters for the location of the exits. She no longer takes lunch in the staff room because someone there uses a particular lemon-scented spray on the tables. She eats alone in a stairwell, and she tells herself this is fine.

She has largely stopped talking about what happened. In the early months, she tried — with Pieter, with her GP, briefly with an occupational health counsellor — but she found that describing the incident only made it more present, not less. So she has built a careful architecture of avoidance around her days. She does not watch medical dramas. She keeps the windows open at home regardless of the weather. She has not been able to return to the particular corridor where it happened, and she has not told her manager this.

What troubles Miriam most, in the quiet moments she allows herself, is not the nightmares or the hypervigilance or even the loneliness of eating in a stairwell. It is the feeling that the woman who has guided thousands of women through the most frightening and transformative moments of their lives can no longer trust the simple act of breathing in.
